rules.title: Since / For
rules.topic: Prepositions of Time with Perfect Tenses
rules.concept: 'Since' is used with a point of time (since 2002, since Monday, since he left) while 'for' is used with a length or period of time (for three years, for two hours). Both normally require a perfect or perfect continuous tense, not a simple present/present continuous or simple past. Expressions like 'from the past two weeks' or 'by three years' are wrong; use 'for the past two weeks' and 'for three years'.

rules.title: Each / Every / Either / Neither / Any / None
rules.concept: 'Each' works both as an adjective and a pronoun, so 'each of the...' is correct; 'every' is only an adjective and cannot act as a subject, so 'every of the...' is wrong. Each and every are always followed by a singular noun and take a singular verb, along with a singular possessive (his/her, not their). 'Either/neither' refer to two things and 'any/none' to more than two, and 'either of/neither of/any of/none of' must be followed by a plural noun with a singular verb.

rules.title: Use of Who / Whom / Whose / Which / That
rules.concept: 'Who' is used for persons as the subject of a verb, while 'whom' is used for persons as the object of a verb or preposition. 'Whose' shows possession or ownership, and must not be confused with 'who's', which is the contraction of 'who is / who was / who has'. 'Which' and 'that' are used for things, animals and non-living nouns, so a person should never be referred to with 'which', nor a thing with 'who'.

rules.title: Modal Verb & Its Uses
rules.concept: Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to, need, dare, used to, had better) are always followed by the bare infinitive (V1) without 'to', except 'ought to', 'used to' and 'have to'. Two modals cannot be used together, and a modal cannot be combined with 'be able to' in the same clause (e.g. 'could not be able to' is wrong). Modals of possibility already carry the sense of probability, so words like 'possibly/likely' must not be added; in purpose clauses 'so that' takes 'may/might/can/could', and 'lest' takes 'should' with no extra negative.

rules.title: Questions Related to Singular & Plural Noun
rules.concept: Certain nouns in English do not change form in the plural or are already plural, so adding '-s' is an error. Words like cattle, furniture, luggage, information, advice, poetry, bricks and equipment are uncountable or collective and take no plural '-s'. Some nouns form plurals irregularly (mice, teeth, oxen, sheep), and in compound nouns the main word is pluralised (mothers-in-law, cupfuls, passers-by, breaks-in).

rules.title: Errors Related to Infinitives
rules.concept: Certain verbs and expressions are followed by a gerund (-ing) rather than an infinitive, and vice versa. Verbs like plan for/settle, hope, recall, prohibit from, take care of, cannot help and let take fixed patterns; 'let' and perception verbs such as 'see' take the bare infinitive without 'to'. Choosing the wrong form between 'to + verb' and 'verb + ing' is the typical error tested.

rules.title: Errors Related to Infinitives
rules.concept: Certain verbs and structures take a bare infinitive rather than 'to + verb'. After causative verbs like make, let, and after 'had better', 'would rather', the infinitive is used without 'to'. Also, some verbs (e.g. prevent, forget in habitual sense, remember for past events) require a gerund or a particular preposition instead of the infinitive, so the wrong form must be spotted and corrected.

rules.title: Uses of Gerund
rules.concept: A gerund (verb + ing) works as a noun and must be used as the subject of a sentence, after prepositions, and after certain verbs and fixed expressions such as 'with a view to', 'look forward to', 'aim at', 'consider', 'persist in', 'take pride in', 'focus on' and 'addicted to'. Using an infinitive or a bare noun form in these positions is an error. Possessive or objective pronouns before the gerund are also part of this structure.

rules.title: Gerund and Infinitive Usage
rules.concept: Certain verbs and expressions such as enjoy, deny, avoid, insist on, look forward to and before/after are followed by a gerund (V+ing), not an infinitive (to + V1). So we say 'enjoy swimming', 'denied taking', 'insist on helping' and 'look forward to meeting'. rules.title: Uses of Participle
rules.concept: Present participles (V+ing) describe something that causes an action or feeling and act actively (an amusing story, a frightening film), while past participles (V3) describe the receiver of the action and act passively (an amused girl, a frightened child). Participles used as adjectives must take their correct form (law-abiding citizens, limited passengers, emerging technology, molten/melted gold). The perfect participle is 'having + V3' (Having paid the fee...), and the participle must logically refer to the subject of the main clause, otherwise it becomes a dangling participle.

rules.title: Articles: No Article in General Sense
rules.concept: When a person or thing is spoken of in a general sense, no article is used before it. So abstract nouns, material nouns and generic plural/uncountable nouns take no article (e.g. 'Man is mortal', 'Honesty is the best policy'). Saying 'The man is mortal' or 'The honesty is the best policy' is therefore wrong.

rules.title: Use of Article Before Proper Nouns
rules.concept: Proper nouns normally take no article, but when a proper noun is used to describe a quality or type, the indefinite article 'a/an' is placed before it (e.g. 'Kalidas is a Shakespeare of India', 'Ahmedabad is becoming a Manchester of India'). Similarly, 'the' is used before a common noun that stands for a quality within a person (e.g. 'The judge in him prevailed upon the father').

rules.title: Articles with Superlative, Comparative Degrees and Ordinals
rules.concept: Use 'the' before superlative degrees and ordinal numbers (the best soldier, the first European sailor). 'The' is also used before a comparative when only two persons/things are compared (of the two, she is the better) and in double comparatives (the more he studied, the greater was his fascination). Note that 'a most' + adjective means 'very' and is not a true superlative.

rules.title: One Article for a Single Entity
rules.concept: When two nouns or adjectives refer to one and the same person/thing regarded as a whole, the article is used only before the first noun/adjective. Repeating the article before the second noun/adjective makes them two separate persons/things. So 'a singer and scientist' means one person, while 'a singer and a scientist' means two people.

rules.title: Omission of Articles in Fixed Phrases
rules.concept: Certain set phrases and idiomatic expressions never take an article, e.g. by mistake, in trouble, in conclusion, at the top of one's voice, set on fire, lose heart, fall silent. Adding 'a/an/the' inside such phrases is an error. Some phrases, however, require the article by convention, e.g. 'in a bad mood', 'in a temper'.

rules.title: Uses of Much / Many / Little / Few
rules.concept: 'Much' and 'little' are used with uncountable nouns, while 'many' and 'few' are used with countable nouns. 'Little/Few' without an article carry a negative sense (almost none), 'a little/a few' carry a positive sense (at least some), and 'the little/the few' mean whatever small quantity remains. Also note 'much' modifies uncountables and comparatives, not adjectives like 'nice' in the positive degree.

rules.title: Many / A Number of / The Number of / More than one
rules.concept: 'Many a' and 'more than one' are followed by a singular noun and a singular verb. 'Many', 'a great many' and 'a number of' take a plural noun with a plural verb, while 'the number of' takes a plural noun but a singular verb. 'More than two' takes a plural noun and plural verb.

rules.title: Use of Double Comparative & Double Superlative
rules.concept: A comparative degree must not be combined with another comparative marker, so 'more better', 'more heavier', 'more warmer' and 'beautifuler' are wrong. Similarly a superlative must not be doubled, as in 'most smartest'. Use either 'more + adjective' or the '-er/-est' form, never both.

rules.title: Errors Related to Active & Passive Voice
rules.concept: In the passive voice the structure must be a form of 'be' plus the past participle (V3), not the -ing form or the bare base form. Intransitive verbs cannot be made passive, so forms like 'are gone', 'were providing' (for 'were provided') and 'has been picked' (for 'has picked') are errors. Choose active or passive according to whether the subject does or receives the action.

rules.title: Verb Agreement with Additive Connectives (With, Along with, As well as)
rules.concept: When two subjects are joined by with, together with, along with, besides, except, including, as well as, unlike, accompanied by, or in addition to, the verb agrees with the first subject only. The words following such connectives are parenthetical and do not change the number of the subject. So a singular first subject takes a singular verb even if the second noun is plural.

rules.title: Correlative Conjunctions: Either-or / Neither-nor / Not only-but also
rules.concept: Correlative conjunctions must be used in their fixed pairs: either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also. With either-or and neither-nor joining two subjects, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. The elements joined by the pair must also be parallel in structure.

rules.title: Hardly/Scarcely ... When; No Sooner ... Than
rules.concept: 'Hardly' and 'Scarcely' are always followed by 'when' (never 'than'), while 'No sooner' is always followed by 'than' (never 'when'). When a sentence begins with Hardly/Scarcely/No sooner, the auxiliary verb must come before the subject (inversion), e.g. 'Hardly had he arrived...', 'No sooner did she see...'. The first clause normally takes past perfect and the second clause simple past.

rules.title: Errors Related to Forms of Verbs
rules.concept: Verbs must appear in the correct form for the tense and structure used; irregular verbs do not take '-ed' (put-put-put, burst-burst-burst, beat-beat-beaten, broadcast-broadcast-broadcast). Commonly confused pairs must be distinguished: rise/raise, lie/lay, fall/fell, hang (hung for objects, hanged for execution), lead/led, find/found (found = establish), flow/overflow, lose/loose and affect/effect. After 'have/has/had' and in passive structures the third form (V3) is required.

rules.title: Correct Use of Verb Forms
rules.concept: Use the correct form of the verb in each structure: after 'has/have/had' use the past participle (V3), after 'did/didn't' and modals use the base form (V1), and after 'is/am/are/was/were' use V-ing or V3 as required. Also distinguish confusable pairs such as rise/raise, lie/lay, hang (hung) for objects vs hanged for people, and bear/bore/borne.

rules.title: Errors based on Quite / Quiet
rules.concept: 'Quite' is an adverb meaning 'completely, fairly, to a considerable degree' and modifies adjectives, adverbs or verbs. 'Quiet' is an adjective/noun meaning silent or calm. Learners commonly write 'quiet' where the intensifier 'quite' is required, e.g. 'quite a generous woman', 'quite badly'. Also, 'quite' should not be combined with another intensifier like 'too'.

rules.title: Errors based on Late / Lately
rules.concept: 'Late' works as both adjective and adverb meaning 'after the expected time' (the train is running late, he came late). 'Lately' means 'recently' and refers to the recent past, usually with the present perfect (he has not been feeling well lately). Using 'lately' for delay, or 'late' for 'recently', is an error.

rules.title: Errors based on Bitter / Bitterly and Sweet / Sweetly
rules.concept: Verbs of sensation such as taste, smell, look, sound and feel are linking verbs and take an adjective, not an adverb, as complement. So we say 'it tasted bitter/sweet', not 'bitterly/sweetly'. The adverb form is used only when the verb shows a real action (she smiled sweetly). Comparatives follow the same rule: 'taste sweeter', not 'more sweetly'.

rules.title: Errors based on Fast / Fastly
rules.concept: 'Fast' serves as both adjective and adverb; there is no word 'fastly' in English. Hence 'he ran so fast', 'running very fast' are correct. Any occurrence of 'fastly' in a sentence is the error part.

rules.title: Errors based on Hard / Hardly
rules.concept: 'Hard' is both adjective and adverb meaning 'with great effort or force' (work hard, hit hard, die hard). 'Hardly' is a negative adverb meaning 'scarcely, almost not', so it reverses the sense of the sentence. There is no word 'hardly' meaning 'with effort', and 'hard-won' (not 'hardly won') is the correct compound adjective.

rules.title: Errors based on Farther / Further
rules.concept: 'Farther' refers to physical or measurable distance (Mumbai is farther from Delhi than Patna). 'Further' is used for additional or extra things that are not physical distance — further information, further punishment, further volumes, further investigation. Substituting 'farther' for abstract addition is the common error.

rules.title: Errors based on Too Much / Much Too
rules.concept: 'Too much' is used with uncountable nouns or after verbs (too much luggage, he talks too much). 'Much too' is an intensifier used before adjectives and adverbs (much too heavy, much too young, much too windy). Writing 'too much' before an adjective, or 'much too' before a noun, is the error.

rules.title: Errors based on Coward/Cowardly, Miser/Miserly, Scholar/Scholarly
rules.concept: Coward, miser and scholar are nouns, while cowardly, miserly and scholarly are the corresponding adjectives. So a person is 'a coward' or behaves 'in a cowardly manner'; 'a coward person' is wrong and should be 'a cowardly person'. Note also that 'cowardly' is an adjective, not an adverb, so 'he behaved cowardly' is incorrect.

rules.title: Subject-Verb Agreement with Main Subject
rules.concept: The verb must agree with the main (head) subject of the sentence, not with any qualifying phrase that follows it. Phrases beginning with 'of', 'with', 'along with', 'containing', 'caused by', etc. are qualifiers and do not change the number of the subject. So 'The crew of sailors was...', 'The box containing the apples was...'. Also, gerunds and abstract nouns as subjects take singular verbs.

rules.title: So / Very / Too / Enough / As-As / So-As
rules.topic: Degrees of Comparison and Adverbs of Degree
rules.concept: 'Very', 'so', 'too' and 'enough' are used with the positive degree, not the comparative: 'very strong', not 'very stronger'. 'Enough' follows the adjective it modifies ('wise enough'), while 'so' is followed by 'that' and 'as...as' is used for positive comparison ('as respectful as'). 'Too' means excessively and also takes the positive degree ('too weak').

rules.title: Use of Superfluous Expressions
rules.concept: Avoid words that repeat meaning already carried by another word in the sentence. Common redundancies include 'discussed about', 'returned back', 'just exactly', 'violate against', 'rest of remaining', 'precedes before', 'approach near', 'supposing if', 'sufficient enough', 'repeat again', 'forbade not to', 'came across with' and 'illustrate about'. Delete the superfluous word to correct the sentence.

rules.title: Use of Conditional Sentences
rules.concept: In conditional sentences the tense of the if-clause controls the tense of the main clause. In the first conditional, 'if + present simple' is followed by 'will + V1' (never 'if ... will'). In the second conditional, 'if + past simple' is followed by 'would + V1', and in the third conditional, 'if + had + V3' is followed by 'would have + V3' (never 'if ... would have'). Similarly, 'as if', 'unless', 'wish' and time clauses take the appropriate past/past perfect or present form rather than 'will/would'.

rules.title: Nouns Joined by a Preposition Stay Singular
rules.concept: When two identical nouns are joined by a preposition (after, to, upon, on), both nouns must remain singular. Correct forms are 'page after page', 'town after town', 'door to door', 'pile upon pile'. Using plural nouns such as 'pages after pages' or 'doors to doors' is an error.

rules.title: Between vs Among
rules.concept: 'Between' is used for two persons or things, while 'among' (or 'amongst') is used for more than two. 'Between' is also used with 'and' (between you and me), never 'among ... and'. With reciprocal pronouns, use 'between ourselves' for two and 'among yourselves/themselves' for more than two.

rules.title: Beside vs Besides
rules.concept: 'Beside' means 'by the side of' or 'next to', indicating physical position. 'Besides' means 'in addition to' or 'apart from'. Note also that neither takes 'of', so 'beside of' is incorrect.

rules.title: Despite / Comprise / Await — No Extra Preposition
rules.concept: 'Despite' is never followed by 'of' (use 'despite' or 'in spite of'). 'Comprise' already means 'consist of', so 'comprises of' or 'comprises from' is wrong; use 'comprises' or 'consists of'. Similarly 'await' takes a direct object, so 'awaiting for' is incorrect — use 'awaiting the results' or 'waiting for the results'.

rules.title: Each Other vs One Another
rules.concept: 'Each other' is used when referring to two persons or things, and 'one another' is used for more than two. Neither expression can be altered to forms like 'one other'.

rules.title: Arrangement of Pronouns
rules.concept: In good news the order of pronouns is 231 (You, he and I), while in confessions of guilt it is 123 (I, you and he). The possessive adjective and reflexive form must agree with the combined subject, so 'You and I have done our best', not 'my best'.

rules.title: Until / Unless
rules.concept: 'Until' refers to time while 'Unless' refers to a condition. Both already carry a negative sense, so a second negative (do not, doesn't, never) must not be used in the same clause. Also, the clause after 'unless/until' takes the present tense, not 'will'.

rules.title: One / ones / one's
rules.concept: When the indefinite pronoun 'one' is the subject, the following pronouns must be 'one', 'one's' or 'oneself', not 'his', 'her' or 'their'. The possessive form is 'one's' with an apostrophe, while the plural substitute 'ones' takes no apostrophe.

rules.title: Both / Between
rules.concept: 'Both' is paired with 'and', never with 'as well as' or 'or'. Similarly 'between' is followed by 'and' and is used for two persons or things, whereas 'among' is used for more than two. Pronouns after 'between' take the objective case (you and me, you and him).

rules.title: No conjunction 'that' before a wh-word
rules.concept: The conjunction 'that' is not used before a wh-word such as how, what, when, why, whether or 'if' in reported speech. Sentences like 'He asked that why he was not selected' are wrong; the 'that' must be dropped. Use either 'that' with a statement clause or the wh-word/if alone with a question clause, never both together.

rules.title: Its/It's, Their/There, Your/Yours
rules.concept: 'Its' is the possessive form while 'it's' means 'it is/has'; 'their' shows possession while 'there' refers to a place or is used in 'there is/are'. 'Your' is used before a noun, whereas 'yours' stands alone as a possessive pronoun and is never followed by a noun. Errors occur when these homophones are interchanged.

rules.title: Errors related to Inversion
rules.concept: Inversion means the auxiliary verb comes before the subject. It is required in interrogative sentences and in clauses beginning with negative or restrictive adverbs such as seldom, never, little, no sooner, under no circumstances, and in 'nor' clauses. For example, 'Never have I listened...' and 'No sooner had she realised...' are correct, while 'Never I have listened' is wrong.

rules.title: Question tags with everyone/everybody/somebody/nobody/nothing
rules.concept: With indefinite pronouns referring to people (everybody, somebody, nobody, anyone), the pronoun used in the question tag is 'they'. With indefinite pronouns referring to things (everything, something, nothing, anything), the tag pronoun is 'it'. Words like nobody and nothing are already negative, so the tag takes a positive verb, e.g. 'Nobody did the work, did they?'

rules.title: Confusion in the usage of nouns and verbs
rules.concept: Some word pairs differ only in whether they are nouns or verbs. 'Practice' and 'advice' are nouns, while 'practise' and 'advise' are verbs. So one gives a piece of advice but advises a friend, and one attends a practice session but practises English daily.

rules.title: Confusing Word Pairs (Spelling & Usage)
rules.concept: Many English word pairs differ by only a letter or two but belong to different parts of speech or meanings, such as practice (noun) / practise (verb), advice (noun) / advise (verb), effect (noun) / affect (verb), complaint (noun) / complain (verb), bath (noun) / bathe (verb), breath (noun) / breathe (verb), licence (noun) / license (verb), lose (verb) / loose (adjective) and elicit (to draw out) / illicit (illegal). Errors occur when the noun form is used where a verb is required or vice versa. Check the grammatical role of the word in the sentence before choosing the spelling.

rules.title: Errors Related to Use of Relative Pronouns 'What' / 'That'
rules.concept: 'That' is a relative pronoun that takes an antecedent (a noun or pronoun before it), whereas 'what' does not take any antecedent and itself means 'the thing which'. So after a stated noun we must use 'that', not 'what'. Using 'what' after an expressed antecedent, as in 'the food what they cooked' or 'the information what I needed', is incorrect.

rules.title: Errors Related to Numeral Adjectives
rules.concept: Numeral adjectives like hundred, thousand, dozen, score and units of measure remain singular when preceded by a definite number (e.g., five hundred people, two dozen mangoes, a five-man committee). They take the plural form with 'of' only when they express an indefinite quantity (hundreds of people, thousands of miles). Similarly, a numeral plus a noun used as a compound adjective stays singular, as in 'five-month-old' and 'five minutes' time' requires the possessive form.

rules.title: Use of Conjunctions: 'if', 'whether' and 'that'
rules.concept: 'If' introduces a condition or an indirect yes/no question, while 'whether' is used when a choice or alternative (often with 'or not') is implied. 'That' introduces a statement or noun clause of certainty and must never be combined with 'if'/'whether' (never 'know that if'). In reported speech, verbs like 'ask' take 'if/whether', not 'that'.

rules.title: Errors Related to Articles (use of 'the')
rules.concept: The definite article 'the' is used before superlative degrees, ordinals and words like former/latter, and in comparative structures of the type 'the more... the better'. Using 'a/an' or omitting the article before a superlative or ordinal ('a best form', 'first time') is an error. Note that with 'most' meaning 'the majority of', no article is used.

rules.title: Article with two subjects forming a single unit
rules.concept: When two nouns joined by 'and' refer to the same person or form a single unit, the article is used only before the first noun and the verb is singular. If the article is repeated before both nouns, they are treated as two separate persons/things and the verb becomes plural. Example: 'The Treasurer and Secretary is present' (one person) vs 'The Treasurer and the Secretary are present' (two people).

rules.title: Idiomatic phrases that do not take articles
rules.concept: Certain fixed idiomatic expressions are used without any article, such as 'by mistake', 'by air', 'in trouble', 'in conclusion', 'set on fire' and 'what sort of people'. Inserting 'a', 'an' or 'the' into these phrases is an error.

rules.title: Errors related to the Apostrophe ('s)
rules.concept: The apostrophe shows possession and must be placed correctly. With compound nouns the 's is added to the last word (sister-in-law's), with joint ownership only the second noun takes 's, and separate ownership requires 's on each noun. Possessive forms of 'somebody else' become 'somebody else's', and double possessives such as 'the poor's' after 'that of' are wrong.

rules.title: Errors related to Parallelism
rules.concept: Words, phrases and clauses joined by coordinating conjunctions or correlative pairs such as 'not only... but also' must be in the same grammatical form. A mismatch of tense, verb form, or structure between the joined elements is an error, as is mixing degrees of comparison in a single parallel series.

rules.title: Errors related to Causative Verbs
rules.concept: The causative verbs have, get, make and let follow fixed patterns. In the active voice, have/make/let take the bare infinitive while get takes 'to + V1'; in the passive voice, have/get take V3 while make/let take 'to + V1'. Examples: 'I made him do the work' / 'He was made to do the work'; 'I got him to do the work' / 'I got the work done by him'.

rules.title: Errors related to Fraction / Percent
rules.concept: With fractions, the verb agrees with the noun that follows 'of' (One third of the birds migrate; Three fourths of the pillar has rotted). Also, the numerator decides the form of the denominator: use singular 'fourth' with 'one/a' and plural 'fourths' when the numerator is more than one (three fourths, two thirds).

rules.title: Errors related to Adjectives — Cardinals, Ordinals, Multiplicatives
rules.concept: When cardinals (one, two), ordinals (first, second) and multiplicatives (single, double) occur together, the correct order is ordinal + cardinal + multiplicative, e.g. 'the first five girls', 'the first two chapters', 'the first two single rooms'. Forms like 'the five first girls' or 'the two first chapters' are incorrect.

rules.title: Arrangement of Adjectives (OSASCOMP)
rules.concept: When several adjectives modify one noun, they follow the OSASCOMP order: Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Colour, Origin, Material, Purpose. So it is 'long blonde hair', 'a big wooden building', 'a small black bag', and 'a small red leather bag'.

rules.title: Made of / Made from
rules.concept: 'Made of' is used when the basic material does not change in the process — a physical change (the table is made of wood; her necklace is made of gold). 'Made from' is used when the basic material changes — a chemical change (curd is made from milk; flour is made from wheat; glass is made from melted sand).

questions.question: They have lived / in this apartment / since ten years.
questions.explanation: 'Ten years' is a length of time, so 'for ten years' must be used instead of 'since ten years'.

questions.question: As it has been raining heavily / since two hours, / the children are / at home.
options: As it has been raining heavily
questions.explanation: 'Two hours' denotes a period of time, so 'for two hours' is correct.

questions.question: Smita lived / in this house / since she was / five years old.
questions.explanation: With 'since', a perfect tense is required: 'Smita has lived / has been living in this house'.

questions.question: She has / not written / a single novel / by three years.
questions.explanation: A length of time takes 'for', so 'for three years' replaces 'by three years'.

questions.question: Elina is / travelling / since / yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Since' needs a perfect continuous tense: 'Elina has been travelling since yesterday'.

questions.question: For the past / three years, / my uncle is / away from home.
questions.explanation: With 'for the past three years' the present perfect is required: 'my uncle has been away from home'.

questions.question: I am working with him since 2002, / but even today / I am unable / to understand his motives.
options: I am working with him since 2002,
questions.explanation: 'Since 2002' requires the present perfect continuous: 'I have been working with him since 2002'.

questions.question: The orphans have been clamouring (a) / for nutritious food (b) / from the past two weeks. (c) / No error, (d)
questions.explanation: 'From the past two weeks' should be 'for the past two weeks', as a duration takes 'for'.

questions.question: We have been / (a) celebrating many festivals / (b) since centuries. / (c) No error (d)
questions.explanation: 'Centuries' is a length of time, so 'for centuries' is correct.

questions.question: The little boy / (a) has been waiting for his turn / (b) since a long time. / (c) No error (d)
options: has been waiting for his turn
questions.explanation: 'A long time' is a duration, so 'for a long time' should be used.

questions.question: No one heard anything / (a) about him since / (b) he left India for good. / (c) No error (d)
questions.explanation: With 'since', the main clause needs the present perfect: 'No one has heard anything'.

questions.question: Since the trip home / (a) was expensive I / (b) did not go home during the holiday. / (c) No error (d)
options: did not go home during the holiday.
questions.explanation: Here 'since' means 'because', so the sentence is correct as it stands.

questions.question: Since his arrival in India, / (a) he is visiting as many villages as he can / (b) to acquire a firsthand knowledge of rural India. / (c) No error, (d)
options: he is visiting as many villages as he can
to acquire a firsthand knowledge of rural India.
questions.explanation: 'Since' requires the present perfect: 'he has been visiting as many villages as he can'.

questions.question: I ate (a) / nothing (b) / since morning, (c) / No error, (d)
questions.explanation: 'Since morning' needs the present perfect: 'I have eaten nothing since morning'.

questions.question: I have been reading books (a) / written by a number of philosophers (b) / since I am a ten year old lad. (c) / No error, (d)
options: written by a number of philosophers
since I am a ten year old lad.
questions.explanation: The clause after 'since' takes the simple past: 'since I was a ten year old lad'.

questions.question: Four years have passed since (a) / we had met each (b) / other in Mumbai, (c) / No error. (d)
questions.explanation: After 'since' the simple past is used: 'we met each other in Mumbai'.

questions.question: Mr. Amit Kumar Singh / had worked with / us since / May 2018.
questions.explanation: 'Since May 2018' requires the present perfect: 'has worked / has been working with us'.

questions.question: My aunt, Sudha, has stitched / dresses for us / every year since / we had been children.
questions.explanation: The clause after 'since' takes the simple past: 'since we were children'.

questions.question: (A) We are living / (B) here since / (C) the summer / (D) of last year.
questions.explanation: With 'since', the present perfect continuous is required: 'We have been living here'.

questions.question: They had been dancing / for an hour / when our dance teacher / had arrived.
questions.explanation: The later action takes the simple past: 'when our dance teacher arrived'.

questions.question: I am working with him since 2002, / but even today / I am unable / to understand his motives.
options: I am working with him since 2002,
questions.explanation: 'Since 2002' requires 'I have been working with him'.

questions.question: I never miss / a cricket match / as I am fond of cricket / since childhood.
options: as I am fond of cricket
questions.explanation: The answer key marks this question as 'No error', which is not among the four printed parts.

questions.question: Every of the five children (1) / standing in the corner (2) / of the room is dexterous in paintings. (3) / No error (4)
options: of the room is dexterous in paintings.
questions.explanation: 'Every' cannot be used as a pronoun; 'Each of the five children' is correct.

questions.question: Every of the two / girls will get / the reward.
questions.explanation: 'Every of' is wrong; use 'Each of the two girls'.

questions.question: The essay is divided / into five paragraphs / and every of these / has seven sentences.
questions.explanation: 'Every of these' should be 'each of these', since 'every' is only an adjective.

questions.question: Every soldier / and every officer / was in / their place.
questions.explanation: 'Every' takes a singular possessive, so 'his place' is required.

questions.question: Every member of the committee (1) / have been present (2) / at all the meetings. (3) / No error (4)
questions.explanation: 'Every member' is singular, so 'has been present' is correct.

questions.question: Each country in the (1) / region have different strengths (2) / and faces different risks (3) / No error (4)
questions.explanation: 'Each country' is singular and takes 'has different strengths'.

questions.question: We are living in a time (1) / where it's a fast life and every individual seem (2) / to be racing like blind (3) / No error (4)
options: We are living in a time
where it's a fast life and every individual seem
questions.explanation: 'Every individual' is singular, so 'seems' is required.

questions.question: The matter (a) / must be considered (b) / from every points of view, (c) / No Error (d)
questions.explanation: 'Every' is followed by a singular noun: 'from every point of view'.

questions.question: I am very thankful to her (a) / as she used to see me at the (b) / hospital every five hour, (c) / No error, (d)
options: I am very thankful to her
as she used to see me at the
questions.explanation: With a plural number after 'every', the noun is plural: 'every five hours'.

questions.question: Every man, woman and child (1) / is now aware of (2) / the terrible consequences of (3) / habit of smoking. (4)
questions.explanation: The article is missing; it should be 'the habit of smoking'.

questions.question: While every care have been taken in preparing the result (a) / the company reserves the right to correct (b) / any inadvertent errors at a later stage, (c) / no error (d)
options: While every care have been taken in preparing the result
the company reserves the right to correct
any inadvertent errors at a later stage,
questions.explanation: 'Every care' is singular, so 'has been taken' is correct.

questions.question: Each of the cast members were (1) / supportive of the director and as a result, (2) / the film was a great success. (3) / No Error (4)
options: Each of the cast members were
supportive of the director and as a result,
the film was a great success.
questions.explanation: 'Each of' takes a singular verb: 'Each of the cast members was'.

questions.question: In our college, it (1) / was obligatory for each of (2) / the student to buy his own instruments. (3) / No Error (4)
options: the student to buy his own instruments.
questions.explanation: 'Each of' must be followed by a plural noun: 'each of the students'.

questions.question: Did you see (1) / any of the child (2) / when you were in the garden? (3) / No Error (4)
options: when you were in the garden?
questions.explanation: 'Any of' takes a plural noun: 'any of the children'.

questions.question: I am certain that none (1) / of these two books (2) / is useful to the students of the 8th standard (3) / No Error (4)
options: is useful to the students of the 8th standard
questions.explanation: 'None' is used for more than two; for two things 'neither of these two books' is correct.

questions.question: The police arrested (A)/ two young men, but (B)/ neither of them were responsible for the robbery. (C)/ No error (D)
options: neither of them were responsible for the robbery.
questions.explanation: 'Neither of them' is singular, so the verb must be 'was', not 'were'.

questions.question: Any of the two pencils will do but it (1)/ must be black in color and its (2)/ length must be shorter. (3)/ No error (4)
options: Any of the two pencils will do but it
must be black in color and its
questions.explanation: For two persons or things 'either' is used, not 'any'; hence 'Either of the two pencils will do'.

questions.question: None of the pens (a)/ that I have purchased (b)/ are working, (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: 'None' followed by a countable plural noun takes a singular verb here, so 'is working' is required.

questions.question: Cows are amongst (a)/ the gentlest of animals (b)/ none shows more passionate tenderness (c)/ towards their young ones. (d)
questions.explanation: 'None' here refers to the plural 'cows/animals', so the plural verb 'show' is needed.

questions.question: I don't recognize (a)/ none of the politicians (b)/ who have been invited to be the speakers today, (c)/ No Error (d)
options: who have been invited to be the speakers today,
questions.explanation: 'Don't' and 'none' together form a double negative; use 'any of the politicians'.

questions.question: My elder brother (a)/ does not smoke (b)/ at all and has no desire neither, (c)/ no error (d)
options: at all and has no desire neither,
questions.explanation: 'No desire neither' is a double negative; it should be 'has no desire either'.

questions.question: Each animals of the same species (1)/ looks for the same sort of food (2)/ also there may be other animals of different species competing with the same food (3)/ No error (4)
options: Each animals of the same species
looks for the same sort of food
also there may be other animals of different species competing with the same food
questions.explanation: 'Each' is followed by a singular noun, so 'Each animal of the same species' is correct.

questions.question: None of the passengers were aware of what (a)/ was going to happen (b)/ in the next two hours, (c)/ no error (d)
options: None of the passengers were aware of what
questions.explanation: 'None of the passengers' takes the singular verb 'was aware' in this construction.

questions.question: Vini bought two new dresses but either is suitable for the festival.
questions.explanation: The negative sense requires 'but neither is suitable', since 'either' cannot convey the intended negation.

questions.question: Neither of the five accused (a)/ was present (b)/ in the court. (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: 'Neither' is used for only two; for more than two use 'None of the five accused'.

questions.question: Neither of them (a)/ did their work (b)/ on time. (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: 'Neither of them' is singular, so the possessive should be 'his work', not 'their work'.

questions.question: My friend / who's leg / was fractured, / has recovered.
questions.explanation: Possession requires 'whose leg'; 'who's' means 'who is/has'.

questions.question: What is the name of the Swami whom autobiography impressed you so much?
questions.explanation: Possession of the autobiography requires 'whose autobiography', not 'whom'.

questions.question: This is the album who I found in the garage.
questions.explanation: 'Album' is a thing, so the relative pronoun must be 'which/that I found'.

questions.question: The government has announced a gradual reboot of air travel who was halted two months ago due to lockdown.
questions.explanation: 'Air travel' is a non-living thing, so 'which was halted' should be used.

questions.question: The master did not know who of the servants had broken the glass.
questions.explanation: Before 'of + noun' the correct form is 'which of the servants'.

questions.question: I work mainly in the computer department, / who is / the smallest department / in the University.
options: I work mainly in the computer department
questions.explanation: 'Department' is a thing, so 'which is' is required instead of 'who is'.

questions.question: My son has brought four pens (a)/ who are red (b)/ in colour, (c)/ no error (d)
options: My son has brought four pens
questions.explanation: Pens are things, so 'which are red' is correct.

questions.question: The government has introduced (a)/ a new law who forces (b)/ farmers to sell their produce only to licensed dealers, (c)/ no error (d)
options: farmers to sell their produce only to licensed dealers,
questions.explanation: 'Law' is a thing; use 'a new law which forces'.

questions.question: The candidate has appealed (1)/ for donations from younger voters, (2)/ who will be used to defray campaign expenses. (3)/ No error (4)
options: who will be used to defray campaign expenses.
questions.explanation: The pronoun refers to 'donations', a thing, so 'which will be used' is correct.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word segment in the following sentence: The girl which is wearing a blue shirt is my sister.
options: which is wearing the blue shirt
who is wearing a blue shirt
questions.explanation: 'Girl' is a person, so the relative pronoun must be 'who', with the singular verb 'is wearing'.

questions.question: The university has ordered (1)/ an inquiry into the leak and formed (2)/ an inquiry committee who will have to submit its primary report within 48 hours (3)/ No Error (4)
options: an inquiry into the leak and formed
an inquiry committee who will have to submit its primary report within 48 hours
questions.explanation: A committee is treated as a thing here, so 'which will have to submit' is correct.

questions.question: Companies who are (1)/ into manufacturing, particularly in the (2)/ gems and stones business, would benefit the most from the new scheme. (3)/ No error (4)
options: gems and stones business, would benefit the most from the new scheme.
questions.explanation: 'Companies' are not persons, so 'Companies which/that are' is required.

questions.question: One day, he decided (1)/ to sculpt a statue of truth (2)/ who he believed would control the behaviour of the people. (3)/ No Error (4)
options: to sculpt a statue of truth
who he believed would control the behaviour of the people.
questions.explanation: The pronoun refers to a statue, a thing, so 'which he believed' is correct.

questions.question: Do you know (a)/ whom the (b)/ next speaker is? (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the complement/subject of 'is', so 'who the next speaker is' is correct.

questions.question: The selection Board will (a)/ call only those (b)/ candidates whom have the proper qualification (c)/ No Error (d)
options: candidates whom have the proper qualification
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'have', so 'candidates who have' is required.

questions.question: On entering the crowded room (a)/ I could not see one person (b)/ who I knew, (c)/ No error (d)
options: I could not see one person
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the object of 'knew', so 'whom I knew' is correct.

questions.question: Rehan and Ronit are / good friends and / it doesn't matter to them / as to whom is wealthier.
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'is wealthier', so 'as to who is wealthier' is correct.

questions.question: Whomever (1)/ comes late will not be allowed (2)/ to mark his presence in the register. (3)/ No Error (4)
options: comes late will not be allowed
to mark his presence in the register.
questions.explanation: As the subject of 'comes', the correct form is 'Whoever'.

questions.question: Whom (a)/ do you plan to invite (b)/ to your party besides Mr. Rao and me? (c)/ no error (d)
options: to your party besides Mr. Rao and me?
questions.explanation: 'Whom' is correctly the object of 'invite', so the sentence has no error.

questions.question: I found this ring (1)/ as I was digging in the (2)/ garden. It looks very old. I wonder to who it belonged. (3)/ No error (4)
options: as I was digging in the
garden. It looks very old. I wonder to who it belonged.
questions.explanation: After the preposition 'to' the object form 'whom' is required: 'to whom it belonged'.

questions.question: We do not know (a)/ whom we should blame (b)/ for all the lapses in the procedure, (c)/ No error (d)
options: for all the lapses in the procedure,
questions.explanation: 'Whom' is the object of 'blame', so the sentence is correct.

questions.question: "I don't understand why I can't come (1)/ to the movies with you," (2)/ cried Tina's younger brother, whom had a strict 8:00 bedtime. (3)/ No error (4)
options: "I don't understand why I can't come
cried Tina's younger brother, whom had a strict 8:00 bedtime.
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'had', so 'who had a strict 8:00 bedtime' is correct.

questions.question: The letter of offer (a)/ is being dispatched to the shareholders of the company (b)/ whom were allotted shares. (c)/ No error (d)
options: is being dispatched to the shareholders of the company
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'were allotted', so 'who were allotted shares' is correct.

questions.question: Please take care of (a)/ whomever is (b)/ waiting. (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'is waiting', so 'whoever is waiting' is correct.

questions.question: A leader is a group member (1)/ which exerts profound influence (2)/ on the behaviour and attitude of other members of the group. (3)/ No error (4)
options: A leader is a group member
on the behaviour and attitude of other members of the group.
questions.explanation: A group member is a person, so 'who exerts profound influence' is required.

questions.question: Passengers (a)/ may not smoke (b)/ inside the plane, (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: Prohibition by rule/law requires 'must not' (or 'cannot'), not 'may not'.

questions.question: He is working (a)/ hard so that he should (b)/ succeed in his mission, (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: 'So that' expressing purpose takes 'may/can' (present context), not 'should'.

questions.question: He expected (a)/ that the problem will be (b)/ sorted out very soon, (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: Past main verb 'expected' requires 'would be' in the subordinate clause.

questions.question: He wished (a)/ that she would (b)/ prosper in life, (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: After 'wish' expressing a blessing/desire, 'might' is used: 'that she might prosper'.

questions.question: He did not help (a)/ me with money (b)/ but he could do it. (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: Unfulfilled past ability needs 'could have done it'.

questions.question: How dare (a)/ you to face (b)/ customers like them? (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: 'Dare' as a modal is followed by the bare infinitive: 'you face'.

questions.question: By the time (a)/ you arrive at the airport (b)/ I will have leave for London, (c)/ no error (d)
options: I will have leave for London
questions.explanation: Future perfect needs the past participle: 'will have left'.

questions.question: He suggested to (a)/ me that we would go to (b)/ watch a movie, (c)/ no error (d)
options: me that we would go to
questions.explanation: After 'suggested', the clause takes 'should go' (or bare subjunctive), not 'would go'.

questions.question: When Veena returned to India she had to get use driving on the left.
questions.explanation: 'Get used to' is followed by a gerund: 'get used to driving'.

questions.question: You had better (a)/ gone (b)/ to school on time. (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: 'Had better' takes the bare infinitive: 'go'.

questions.question: You had better (a)/ to stop taking medicine (b)/ which have side effect. (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: 'Had better' is followed by V1 without 'to': 'stop taking'.

questions.question: The members (a)/ may possibly (b)/ attend the party. (c)/ no error (d)
questions.explanation: 'May' already expresses possibility, so 'possibly' is redundant.

questions.question: Because of the heavy rain (a)/ students could not be able to (b)/ attend the meeting. (c)/ no error (d)
options: students could not be able to
questions.explanation: A modal cannot combine with 'be able to'; use 'could not attend' or 'were not able to attend'.

questions.question: Radha woke up early that morning so that she should watch the beautiful sunrise.
questions.explanation: With a past main clause, 'so that' takes 'might/could', not 'should'.

questions.question: A historian envisions a future in which humans cannot be able to survive at all if they do not remain connected.
options: not be able to survive at all
can be able to survive at all
will not be able to survive at all
questions.explanation: 'Cannot be able to' is wrong; the future reference requires 'will not be able to survive'.

questions.question: You should not be (1)/ so quick in giving (2)/ advice, lest you will be perceived as interfering in others' affairs (3)/ No Error (4)
options: advice, lest you will be perceived as interfering in others' affairs
questions.explanation: 'Lest' is followed by 'should', not 'will'.

questions.question: The available statistics (1)/ indicate that the population of the world will double in about 30 years (2)/ and human life will became more and more miserable. (3)/ No Error (4)
options: indicate that the population of the world will double in about 30 years
and human life will became more and more miserable
questions.explanation: After 'will', the bare infinitive is required: 'will become'.

questions.question: You must (1)/ not held in high esteem (2)/ those who are danger to our society. (3)/ No Error (4)
options: those who are danger to our society
questions.explanation: 'Must' takes V1: 'must not hold in high esteem'.

questions.question: This will explains the decision taken (1)/ to impose a blockade on the country in (2)/ the midst of a crisis. (3)/ No error (4)
options: This will explains the decision taken
to impose a blockade on the country in
questions.explanation: 'Will' must be followed by 'explain', not 'explains'.

questions.question: He used to sits day and night (1)/ under a tree in front of a temple (2)/ that is how he earned the name. (3)/ No error (4)
options: He used to sits day and night
under a tree in front of a temple
that is how he earned the name
questions.explanation: 'Used to' is followed by V1: 'used to sit'.

questions.question: I remember my childhood days (A)/ when I was used to go (B)/ to the farm with my father and help him in his work. (C)/ No error (D)
options: when I was used to go
to the farm with my father and help him in his work
questions.explanation: Past habit is expressed by 'used to go', not 'was used to go'.

questions.question: The doctor advised Mr. Murugan that, (A)/ because of his severe cramps, (B)/ he should lay in the bed for a few days. (C)/ No error (D)
options: The doctor advised Mr. Murugan that,
he should lay in the bed for a few days
questions.explanation: The intransitive verb 'lie' is needed: 'should lie in bed'.

questions.question: I would always (A)/ cherished the fond (B)/ memories of our association. (C)/ No error (D)
questions.explanation: 'Would' takes V1: 'cherish'.

questions.question: She will being studying for her exams tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Future continuous is 'will be studying', not 'will being studying'.

questions.question: She shall being / travelling / by this time / tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Correct form is 'She shall be travelling'.

questions.question: Shall you like (a)/ to accompany us in the picnic which (b)/ we are going to arrange today? (c)/ no error (d)
options: to accompany us in the picnic which
we are going to arrange today?
questions.explanation: For a polite invitation/request, 'Would you like' is correct.

questions.question: The criminal (a)/ dare not to go out (b)/ because he is afraid of being recognised by the police, (c)/ No error (d)
options: because he is afraid of being recognised by the police
questions.explanation: Modal 'dare not' takes the bare infinitive: 'dare not go out'.

questions.question: At the end of the day, / cinema ought to helped us / recognize characters as fellow human beings.
options: At the end of the day,
recognize characters as fellow human beings
questions.explanation: 'Ought to' is followed by V1: 'ought to help us'.

questions.question: The first meeting of the Standing Committee will be hold next week.
questions.explanation: Future passive requires the past participle: 'will be held'.

questions.question: Would you have been so kind as to close the window?
questions.explanation: A polite present request takes 'Would you be so kind as to...'.

questions.question: Keep him at arm's length lest you may not repent in the long run.
questions.explanation: 'Lest' is followed by 'should' and is already negative, so 'not' is dropped.

questions.question: He is above eighty (a)/ and dares not read (b)/ without glasses, (c)/ No Error (d)
questions.explanation: As a modal, 'dare' takes no '-s': 'dare not read'.

questions.question: Need I to (a)/ wait (b)/ for your approval? (c)/ No Error (d)
questions.explanation: Modal 'need' in questions takes the bare infinitive: 'Need I wait'.

questions.question: You need not tell a lie (A)/ when the judge asked you where you were (B)/ when the crime was committed. (C)/ No error. (D)
options: You need not tell a lie
when the judge asked you where you were
questions.explanation: Past context requires 'need not have told a lie'.

questions.question: You should / have respond / to my query / sooner.
questions.explanation: 'Should have' takes the past participle: 'have responded'.

questions.question: We all will be shift to our new house next month.
questions.explanation: Correct form is 'will be shifting' (or 'will shift').

questions.question: I will be gone to buy a cupboard which will fit under the stairs.
questions.explanation: Planned future intention is expressed by 'am going to buy'.

questions.question: Will Ramya / had completed / that work / by 2025?
questions.explanation: Future perfect requires 'have completed', not 'had completed'.

questions.question: We will / have been know the result / of the CAT exam by next week.
options: of the CAT exam by next week
questions.explanation: Correct form is 'will have known the result'.

questions.question: Are you sure that / you will be broadcast / the news to everyone / across the country?
questions.explanation: Active future needs 'you will broadcast' (or 'will be broadcasting').

questions.question: Black holes can has powerful effects on their surroundings.
questions.explanation: After the modal 'can', use V1: 'have powerful effects'.

questions.question: These stray cattles are roaming around the town.
questions.explanation: 'Cattle' is already plural; 'cattles' is incorrect.

questions.question: This furnitures has been taken on hire for the function in the college.
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and has no plural form.

questions.question: I think all our furniture needing to be polished.
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is uncountable and takes a singular verb: 'needs to be polished'.

questions.question: When we arrived at Jhansi station (a) / we kept our (b) / luggages in the cloak room. (c) / no error (d)
options: When we arrived at Jhansi station
questions.explanation: 'Luggage' is uncountable; 'luggages' is incorrect.

questions.question: My professor gave me a lot of useful advices when I was writing my research paper.
options: gave me a lots of useful advices
gave me a lot of useful advice
give me lots of useful advices
questions.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable, so 'a lot of useful advice' is correct.

questions.question: I had no informations about the bank strike so I went there yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Information' is uncountable and cannot be pluralised.

questions.question: The mother-in-laws (a) / gathered together to discuss (b) / certain family issues that had to be sorted out. (c) / No error (d)
options: certain family issues that had to be sorted out.
questions.explanation: The plural of 'mother-in-law' is 'mothers-in-law'.

questions.question: It is harmful to take cupsful (a) / of tea (b) / five times a day. (c) / no error (d)
options: It is harmful to take cupsful
questions.explanation: The correct plural is 'cupfuls', not 'cupsful'.

questions.question: The brethrens of this locality are always (a) / at daggers-drawn without any (b) / apparent reason. (c) / no error (d)
options: The brethrens of this locality are always
questions.explanation: 'Brethren' is already plural; 'brethrens' is incorrect.

questions.question: "I know nothing (a) / about his whereabout. Do you? " (b) / he said to me. (c) / no error (d)
questions.explanation: The noun is always plural: 'whereabouts'.

questions.question: Most of the poultries (a) / consumed in India (b) / come from Bangladesh, (c) / No error (d)
questions.explanation: 'Poultry' is uncountable and has no plural form.

questions.question: Women athletes have (1) / performed far better (2) / than man athletes this sport season. (3) / No error (4)
options: than man athletes this sport season.
questions.explanation: It should be 'men athletes' to match the plural 'athletes'.

questions.question: Darts are (1) / played by (2) / men as well as women. (3) / No Error (4)
questions.explanation: 'Darts' is the name of a game and takes a singular verb: 'Darts is'.

questions.question: Sheeps are economically useful (1) / and so they are reared (2) / in the hills (3) / No error (4)
questions.explanation: 'Sheep' has the same form in singular and plural.

questions.question: The haves should not look scornfully (a) / at the haves not, rather they should (b) / try to encourage them to work hard and earn their livelihood, (c) / no error (d)
options: The haves should not look scornfully
at the haves not, rather they should
try to encourage them to work hard and earn their livelihood,
questions.explanation: The correct expression is 'the have-nots'.

questions.question: When you see his (a) / offsprings, you can't (b) / believe that he is above seventy, (c) / no error (d)
options: believe that he is above seventy,
questions.explanation: 'Offspring' is the same in singular and plural.

questions.question: Wordsworth's poetries (a) / is characterised by his subtle description (b) / of the beauty and liveliness of Nature, (c) / no error (d)
options: is characterised by his subtle description
of the beauty and liveliness of Nature,
questions.explanation: 'Poetry' is uncountable and has no plural form.

questions.question: People blamed him (1) / for being (2) / a coward person. (3) / No Error (4)
questions.explanation: 'Coward' is a noun; 'a coward' alone is correct, or the adjective 'cowardly person'.

questions.question: The manager of the hotel (a) / requested the boarder to mention (b) / his whereabout in the register. (c) / no error (d)
questions.explanation: The noun is always plural: 'whereabouts'.

questions.question: There have been / three breaks-in / in our society / this month.
questions.explanation: The plural of 'break-in' is 'break-ins'.

questions.question: The manager told / the staff to complete / all the works / before going home.
questions.explanation: 'Work' in this sense is uncountable: 'all the work'.

questions.question: Last month, / we purchased / electronic equipments from / a European country.
questions.explanation: 'Equipment' is uncountable and has no plural form.

questions.question: Language consists of several stratums said a linguist (1) / in his lecture on Language (2) / and Linguistics. (3) / no error (4)
options: Language consists of several stratums said a linguist
questions.explanation: The plural of 'stratum' is 'strata'.

questions.question: He knocked out (1) / four tooths of his assailant (2) / with a single punch that night. (3) / No error (4)
options: with a single punch that night.
questions.explanation: The plural of 'tooth' is 'teeth'.

questions.question: The wall of this magnificent (1) / building is (2) / fifty foot high and its paintings are very striking. (3) / No Error (4)
